<!-- Definition and symptoms -->
'''Uterine atony''' is the failure of the [[uterus]] to contract adequately following [[delivery]].<ref name=Stat2020/> Symptoms can include [[post partum bleeding]], of which it is the causes in more than 75% of cases.<ref name=Stat2020>{{cite journal | vauthors = Gill P, Patel A, Van Hook JW | title = Uterine Atony | date = 2020 | pmid = 29630290 | url = https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK493238/ | access-date = 2020-10-19 | publisher = StatPearls Publishing | journal = StatPearls | place = Treasure Island (FL) | archive-date = 2021-08-27 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174413/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK493238/ | url-status = live }}  [[File:CC-BY icon.svg|50px]]  Text was copied from this source, which is available under a [https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016050101/https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ |date=2017-10-16 }}.</ref> Complications may include [[anemia]] and [[iron deficiency]].<ref name=Stat2020/>

<!-- Cause and diagnosis -->
Risk factors include [[prolonged labor]], [[precipitous labor]], uterine distension (twins, [[polyhydramnios]], [[large for gestational age]]), [[fibroids]], [[body mass index|BMI]] > 40, and [[chorioamnionitis]].<ref name=Stat2020/> Contraction of the muscles of the uterus is required to close the blood vessels that supply were the [[placenta]] attaches after its delivery.<ref name=Stat2020/> Diagnosis is by feeling the uterus following delivery.<ref name=Stat2020/> Other conditions that may present similarly include [[retained placenta]], [[uterine inversion]], and lacerations associated with delivery.<ref name=Stat2020/>

<!-- Prevention, treatment, and epidemiology -->
Blood products should be ready for us in those at high risk.<ref name=Stat2020/> [[Oxytocin (medication)|Oxytocin]] may also be given to try to prevent its occurrence.<ref name=Stat2020/> Treatment may include [[uterine massage]], medications, uterus packing, or surgery.<ref name=Stat2020/> Medications used include oxytocin, [[methylergometrine]], [[carboprost]], [[misoprostol]], and [[prostaglandin E2]].<ref name=Stat2020/><ref name=Bi2021>{{cite journal |last1=Bienstock |first1=JL |last2=Eke |first2=AC |last3=Hueppchen |first3=NA |title=Postpartum Hemorrhage. |journal=The New England journal of medicine |date=29 April 2021 |volume=384 |issue=17 |pages=1635-1645 |doi=10.1056/NEJMra1513247 |pmid=33913640}}</ref> Uterine atony occurs in 2.5% of deliveries in the United States.<ref name=Stat2020/> Globally postpartum bleeding is a top 5 causes of [[maternal death]].<ref name=Coch2014>{{cite journal | vauthors = Mousa HA, Blum J, Abou El Senoun G, Shakur H, Alfirevic Z | title = Treatment for primary postpartum haemorrhage | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | issue = 2 | pages = CD003249 | date = February 2014 | pmid = 24523225 | pmc = 6483801 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD003249.pub3 | collaboration = Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group }}</ref>

==Signs and symptoms==
Symptoms of uterine atony can include [[post partum bleeding]].

=== Complications ===
PPH can cause complications including:<ref name=Coch2014/><ref name=":5" />

* death
* [[hypovolemic shock]]
* [[Disseminated intravascular coagulation|disseminated intravascular coagulopathy]]
* kidney failure
* liver failure
* [[Acute respiratory distress syndrome|adult respiratory distress syndrome]]

In low‐income countries there are several other factors that play a role in PPH risk. Poor nutritional status, lack of healthcare access, and limited blood product supply are additional factors that increase morbidity and mortality.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Khan KS, Wojdyla D, Say L, Gülmezoglu AM, Van Look PF | title = WHO analysis of causes of maternal death: a systematic review | journal = Lancet | volume = 367 | issue = 9516 | pages = 1066–1074 | date = April 2006 | pmid = 16581405 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(06)68397-9 | s2cid = 2190885 }}</ref>

Postpartum anemia is common after an episode of uterine atony and postpartum hemorrhage.<ref name=Stat2020 /> Severe anemia due to PPH may require red cell transfusions, depending on the severity of anemia and the degree of symptomatology attributable to anemia. A common practice is to offer a transfusion to symptomatic women with a hemoglobin value less than 7 g/dL. In most cases of uterine atony-related postpartum hemorrhage, the amount of iron lost is not fully replaced by the transfused blood. Oral iron should thus be also considered. Parenteral iron therapy is an option as it accelerated recovery. Most women with mild to moderate anemia, however, resolve the anemia sufficiently rapidly with oral iron alone and do not need parenteral iron.<ref name=Stat2020/><ref name=Coch2014/>

==Risk factors==
There are many risk factors for uterine atony and several are due to the type of labor a mother experiences such as prolonged labor, labor lasting less than 3 hours, uterine inversion, the use of magnesium sulfate infusions, and extended use of oxytocin. Uterine distention caused by things like more than one fetus present, [[polyhydramnios]], f[[Large for gestational age|etal macrosomia]], uterine fibroids, [[chorioamnionitis]] can also lead to decreased uterine function and atony. Retained placental tissue or placental disorders, such as an adherent placenta, [[Placenta praevia|placenta previa]], and [[Placental abruption|abruption placentae]] increase the mother's risk of PPH.  Body mass index (BMI) above 40 and [[coagulopathy|coagulopathies]] are known risk factors.<ref name=Stat2020 /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Breathnach F, Geary M | title = Uterine atony: definition, prevention, nonsurgical management, and uterine tamponade | journal = Seminars in Perinatology | volume = 33 | issue = 2 | pages = 82–7 | date = April 2009 | pmid = 19324236 | doi = 10.1053/j.semperi.2008.12.001 }}</ref><ref name=Coch2014/><ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last1=Wetta|first1=Luisa A.|last2=Szychowski|first2=Jeff M.|last3=Seals|first3=Samantha|last4=Mancuso|first4=Melissa S.|last5=Biggio|first5=Joseph R.|last6=Tita|first6=Alan T. N.|date=2013|title=Risk factors for uterine atony/postpartum hemorrhage requiring treatment after vaginal delivery|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23507549|journal=American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology|volume=209|issue=1|pages=51.e1–6|doi=10.1016/j.ajog.2013.03.011|issn=1097-6868|pmc=3788839|pmid=23507549|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2021-04-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420103947/https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23507549/|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Magnesium sulfate (medical use)|Magnesium sulfate]] is used often in people with [[Pre-eclampsia|preeclampsia]] and [[eclampsia]], can inadvertently inhibit uterine contractions. In addition, preeclampsia can lead to blood disorders such as  [[thrombocytopenia]], platelet abnormalities, and [[disseminated intravascular coagulation]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ciobanu|first1=Anca Marina|last2=Colibaba|first2=Simona|last3=Cimpoca|first3=Brandusa|last4=Peltecu|first4=Gheorghe|last5=Panaitescu|first5=Anca Maria|date=2016|title=Thrombocytopenia in Pregnancy|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28465752|journal=Maedica|volume=11|issue=1|pages=55–60|issn=1841-9038|pmc=5394486|pmid=28465752|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2021-04-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420104311/https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28465752/|url-status=live}}</ref>. Cesarean delivery, especially after prolonged labor, may cause the muscles of the uterus to become tired and stop contracting or contraction can be inhibited at the surgical site.<ref name=Coch2014/>

== Pathophysiology ==
The uterus is composed of a interconnected muscle fibers known as the [[myometrium]]. The blood vessels that provide the blood supply to the placenta pass through this muscle.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal | vauthors = Baskett TF | title = A flux of the reds: evolution of active management of the third stage of labour | journal = Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine | volume = 93 | issue = 9 | pages = 489–93 | date = September 2000 | pmid = 11089490 | pmc = 1298111 | doi = 10.1177/014107680009300913 | url = https://doi.org/10.1177/014107680009300913 | access-date = 2020-10-19 | archive-date = 2021-08-27 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174357/https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/014107680009300913 | url-status = live }}</ref>  After labor it is the contraction of these muscles that physically squeeze the blood vessels so that [[hemostasis]] can occur after the delivery of the fetus and the placenta.<ref name=Stat2020 />  Local hemostatic factors like [[TNF inhibitor|tissue factor type-1 plasminogen activator inhibitor]] and platelets and clotting factors aid in stopping the blood flow.<REF name=Stat2020/><ref name=":3" />

This physiological contraction does not occur if the myometrium becomes atonic. [[Oxytocin]] is released continuously during labor to stimulate uterine muscle contraction so the that the fetus can be delivered and it is continued to be released after delivery to stop blood flow.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Belghiti|first1=J.|last2=Kayem|first2=G.|last3=Dupont|first3=C.|last4=Rudigoz|first4=R.-C.|last5=Bouvier-Colle|first5=M.-H.|last6=Deneux-Tharaux|first6=C.|date=2011-12-21|title=Oxytocin during labour and risk of severe postpartum haemorrhage: a population-based, cohort-nested case-control study|url=https://bmjopen.bmj.com/lookup/doi/10.1136/bmjopen-2011-000514|journal=BMJ Open|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|pages=e000514|doi=10.1136/bmjopen-2011-000514|issn=2044-6055|pmc=3334825|pmid=22189353|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2021-08-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174407/https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/1/2/e000514|url-status=live}}</ref>  If the oxytocin receptors become desensitized and no longer respond to the hormone then the uterus does not contract.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Belghiti|first1=J.|last2=Kayem|first2=G.|last3=Dupont|first3=C.|last4=Rudigoz|first4=R.-C.|last5=Bouvier-Colle|first5=M.-H.|last6=Deneux-Tharaux|first6=C.|date=2011-12-21|title=Oxytocin during labour and risk of severe postpartum haemorrhage: a population-based, cohort-nested case-control study|url=https://bmjopen.bmj.com/lookup/doi/10.1136/bmjopen-2011-000514|journal=BMJ Open|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|pages=e000514|doi=10.1136/bmjopen-2011-000514|issn=2044-6055|pmc=3334825|pmid=22189353|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2021-08-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174407/https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/1/2/e000514|url-status=live}}</ref> The uterus can also be structurally damaged or distended to prevent contraction. Therefore, as placenta is delivered [[Spiral artery|arteries]] are damaged and without the muscle contractions hemostasis cannot be reached.<ref name=Stat2020 />

Blood loss is an expected part of labor and less than 500 mL is considered normal.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ripley DL | title = Uterine emergencies. Atony, inversion, and rupture | journal = Obstetrics and Gynecology Clinics of North America | volume = 26 | issue = 3 | pages = 419–34, vii | date = September 1999 | pmid = 10472062 | doi = 10.1016/S0889-8545(05)70087-5 | url = http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0889854505700875 | access-date = 2020-10-19 | archive-date = 2021-08-27 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174453/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0889854505700875 | url-status = live }}</ref> Generally, primary PPH is classified as being more than 500 mL of blood lost in the first 24 hours following delivery.<ref name=Coch2014/> Those who have a caesarean section typically have more blood loss than a vaginal birth; so 1000 mL is commonly used to determine excessive blood loss. It is easy to underestimate maternal blood loss because the primary method of assessment is visual observation.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal | vauthors = Sloan NL, Durocher J, Aldrich T, Blum J, Winikoff B | title = What measured blood loss tells us about postpartum bleeding: a systematic review | journal = BJOG | volume = 117 | issue = 7 | pages = 788–800 | date = June 2010 | pmid = 20406227 | pmc = 2878601 | doi = 10.1111/j.1471-0528.2010.02567.x | url = https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1471-0528.2010.02567.x%4010.1002/%28ISSN%291471-0528%28CAT%29EditorsPick%28VI%29EditorsPick | url-status = dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Stafford I, Dildy GA, Clark SL, Belfort MA | title = Visually estimated and calculated blood loss in vaginal and cesarean delivery | journal = American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology | volume = 199 | issue = 5 | pages = 519.e1–7 | date = November 2008 | pmid = 18639209 | doi = 10.1016/j.ajog.2008.04.049 | url = http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0002937808005012 | access-date = 2020-10-19 | archive-date = 2021-08-27 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174428/https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0002937808005012 | url-status = live }}</ref>

== Diagnosis ==
Identifying risk factors early in the pregnancy is essential in managing uterine atony and PPH.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bateman BT, Berman MF, Riley LE, Leffert LR | title = The epidemiology of postpartum hemorrhage in a large, nationwide sample of deliveries | language = en-US | journal = Anesthesia and Analgesia | volume = 110 | issue = 5 | pages = 1368–73 | date = May 2010 | pmid = 20237047 | doi = 10.1213/ANE.0b013e3181d74898 | s2cid = 46459480 }}</ref> This allows for planning and organizing the necessary resources including staff, medicines, assistive devices, and the proper blood products. The delivery plan should also be cognizant of the ability of the hospital or facility to provide an appropriate level of care if any complications occur.<REF name=Stat2020/>

Most diagnosis of uterine atony are made during the physical exam directly upon completion of the delivery. Diffuse uterine atony is typically diagnosed by patient observation rather than blood loss. The uterus can be directly palpated or observed indirectly using a [[bimanual examination]] post delivery. An atonic uterus can feel soft, "boggy" and/or enlarged.<ref name=Coch2014/> Bleeding from the [[Cervix|cervical os]] is also common. If the atony is localized to one area of the uterus, the [[Uterine fundus|upper, fundal]] region may be still be squeezing while the lower uterine segment is non functional. This can be difficult to see with a cursory abdominal examination and easily overlooked. Therefore, a comprehensive vaginal, abdominal, and rectal examination should be performed. The physical examination may include  [[ultrasound]] imaging for rapid visualization of the uterus and other causes of bleeding.<REF name=Stat2020/> Expulsion of gestational products such as the [[placenta]] and rapid identification of obstetric lacerations, helps exclude other causes of PPH.<ref name=Stat2020 /> Laboratory tests can be drawn if coagulopathies are suspected.

Before delivery all people should be screened for risk factors and then assigned a postpartum bleeding risk stratification based on the [[American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists]] recommendations. If the woman is at a medium risk, blood should be [[Packed red blood cells|typed and screened]]. Those assessed to be high risk should be [[Type and cross|typed and cross-matched]].<REF name=Stat2020/><ref name=":5">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hussain SA, Guarini CB, Blosser C, Poole AT | title = Obstetric Hemorrhage Outcomes by Intrapartum Risk Stratification at a Single Tertiary Care Center | journal = Cureus | volume = 11 | issue = 12 | pages = e6456 | date = December 2019 | pmid = 32025387 | pmc = 6977573 | doi = 10.7759/cureus.6456 | url = https://www.cureus.com/articles/25349-obstetric-hemorrhage-outcomes-by-intrapartum-risk-stratification-at-a-single-tertiary-care-center | access-date = 2020-10-20 | archive-date = 2020-10-24 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201024210835/https://www.cureus.com/articles/25349-obstetric-hemorrhage-outcomes-by-intrapartum-risk-stratification-at-a-single-tertiary-care-center | url-status = live }}</ref>

Active management of the [[Placental expulsion|third stage of labor]] is routinely implemented and is considered the standard for patient care. It can be utilized to reduce the risk of PPH.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McDonald S | title = Management of the third stage of labor | journal = Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health | volume = 52 | issue = 3 | pages = 254–61 | date = 2007-05-01 | pmid = 17467592 | doi = 10.1016/j.jmwh.2007.02.012 | series = Special Continuing Education Issue on Intrapartum Care }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Anderson|first1=Janice M.|last2=Etches|first2=Duncan|date=2007-03-15|title=Prevention and management of postpartum hemorrhage|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17390600|journal=American Family Physician|volume=75|issue=6|pages=875–882|issn=0002-838X|pmid=17390600|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2021-04-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420103056/https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17390600/|url-status=live}}</ref> Active management of the third stage includes uterine massage and a IV low dose oxytocin. Whether it is given just before or after the delivery of the placenta is subject to provider preference.<REF name=Stat2020/> It is suggested that using an [[uterotonic]], such as oxytocin, prophylactically will help reduce blood loss and the need for a blood transfusion after delivery.<ref name=":6">{{cite journal | vauthors = Begley CM, Gyte GM, Devane D, McGuire W, Weeks A, Biesty LM | veditors = Begley CM | title = Active versus expectant management for women in the third stage of labour | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | volume = 2 | pages = CD007412 | date = February 2019 | pmid = 30754073 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.cd007412 | publisher = John Wiley & Sons, Ltd | pmc = 6372362 | place = Chichester, UK | collaboration = The Cochrane Collaboration }}</ref>

A uterine massage is performed by placing a hand on the lower abdomen and using repetitive massaging or squeezing movements in attempt to stimulate the uterus. It is theorized, the massaging motion stimulates uterine contraction and may also trigger the release of local [[prostaglandin]]<nowiki/>s to help hemostasis.<ref>{{Cite web|title=WHO recommendation on the use of uterine massage for the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage {{!}} RHL|url=https://extranet.who.int/rhl/topics/preconception-pregnancy-childbirth-and-postpartum-care/postpartum-care/postpartum-haemorrhage/who-recommendation-use-uterine-massage-treatment-postpartum-haemorrhage|access-date=2020-10-20|website=extranet.who.int|language=en|archive-date=2020-10-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201021102356/https://extranet.who.int/rhl/topics/preconception-pregnancy-childbirth-and-postpartum-care/postpartum-care/postpartum-haemorrhage/who-recommendation-use-uterine-massage-treatment-postpartum-haemorrhage|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Treatment==
If uterine atony occurs even after all preventative measures have been taken, medical management should be implemented. Uterine [[fundal massage]] and compression should be maintained, while while medications are given.<ref name=Stat2020/> An intravenous catheter should be started to administer fluids, medications, and blood products.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = El Senoun GA, Singh M, Mousa HA, Alfirevic Z |date= November 2011 |title= Update on the new modalities on the prevention and management of postpartum haemorrhage |journal=Fetal and Maternal Medicine Review |volume=22|issue=4|pages=247–264|doi=10.1017/S0965539511000143|issn=0965-5395}}</ref>

===Medications===
There are several different types of uterotonic medications that may be given, and the each has their own advantages and disadvantages.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = McDonald S, Abbott JM, Higgins SP | title = Prophylactic ergometrine-oxytocin versus oxytocin for the third stage of labour | journal = The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews | issue = 1 | pages = CD000201 | date = 2004 | pmid = 14973949 | pmc = 6491201 | doi = 10.1002/14651858.CD000201.pub2 | collaboration = Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group }}</ref> Moreover, the use of combination uterotonic therapy is a common practice and might be more effective at controlling bleeding than a single medication. Some combinations might include oxytocin plus misoprostol, oxytocin plus ergometrine, and carbetocin.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last1=Gallos|first1=Ioannis D|last2=Williams|first2=Helen M|last3=Price|first3=Malcolm J|last4=Merriel|first4=Abi|last5=Gee|first5=Harold|last6=Lissauer|first6=David|last7=Moorthy|first7=Vidhya|last8=Tobias|first8=Aurelio|last9=Deeks|first9=Jonathan J|last10=Widmer|first10=Mariana|last11=Tunçalp|first11=Özge|date=2018-04-25|editor-last=Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group|title=Uterotonic agents for preventing postpartum haemorrhage: a network meta-analysis|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/14651858.CD011689.pub2|journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews|volume=4|pages=CD011689|language=en|doi=10.1002/14651858.CD011689.pub2|pmc=6494487|pmid=29693726|access-date=2020-10-22|archive-date=2021-08-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174436/https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD011689.pub2/full|url-status=live}}</ref>

Medications used often include the following:<REF name=Stat2020/><ref name=Coch2014/>

* [[Oxytocin (medication)|Oxytocin]] 5 to 10 IU IM or 10 to 40 units intravenous.<ref name=Bi2021/> Stimulation of oxytocin receptors in the uterine muscle leads to contractions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dyer|first1=R.A.|last2=van Dyk|first2=D.|last3=Dresner|first3=A.|date=2010|title=The use of uterotonic drugs during caesarean section|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0959289X10000592|journal=International Journal of Obstetric Anesthesia|language=en|volume=19|issue=3|pages=313–319|doi=10.1016/j.ijoa.2010.04.011|pmid=20627531|access-date=2020-10-22|archive-date=2018-07-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180702011452/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0959289X10000592|url-status=live}}</ref> The number of these receptors increases during pregnancy and with labor. There are also more in the fundus than in the lower uterine segment.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=ARIAS|first=FERNANDO|date=2000|title=Pharmacology of Oxytocin and Prostaglandins|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1097/00003081-200009000-00006|journal=Clinical Obstetrics and Gynecology|volume=43|issue=3|pages=455–468|doi=10.1097/00003081-200009000-00006|pmid=10949750|issn=0009-9201|access-date=2020-10-22|archive-date=2021-08-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174403/https://journals.lww.com/clinicalobgyn/Citation/2000/09000/Pharmacology_of_Oxytocin_and_Prostaglandins.6.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref> Oxytocin has a quick onset of action, within a few minutes, but also loses effectiveness quickly because of a short half-life.The medicine is given in a rapid infusion and may cause hypotension. Oxytocin alone is the usually treatment of atony in the US. However, if bleeding is uncontrolled  after administration of oxytocin, then a second uterotonic is given. <ref name=":8" />
*[[Methylergometrine]] 0.2 mg IM or by mouth.<ref name=Bi2021/> This is an ergot alkaloid and has multiple mechanisms of action to induce fast, regular uterine contractions which leads to sustained uterine contraction.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=den Hertog|first1=C.E.C.|last2=de Groot|first2=A.N.J.A.|last3=van Dongen|first3=P.W.J.|date=2001|title=History and use of oxytocics|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0301211500003110|journal=European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology|language=en|volume=94|issue=1|pages=8–12|doi=10.1016/S0301-2115(00)00311-0|pmid=11134819|access-date=2020-10-22|archive-date=2018-06-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626151538/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0301211500003110|url-status=live}}</ref> It can cause peripheral vasoconstriction and is contraindicated in people with hypertension or pregnancy related hypertension.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Butwick|first1=Alexander J.|last2=Carvalho|first2=Brendan|last3=Blumenfeld|first3=Yair J.|last4=El-Sayed|first4=Yasser Y.|last5=Nelson|first5=Lorene M.|last6=Bateman|first6=Brian T.|date=2015|title=Second-line uterotonics and the risk of hemorrhage-related morbidity|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25582104|journal=American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology|volume=212|issue=5|pages=642.e1–7|doi=10.1016/j.ajog.2015.01.008|issn=1097-6868|pmc=4416982|pmid=25582104|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2020-10-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027145354/https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25582104/|url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Carboprost]] 0.25 mg every 15 to 90 min IM.<ref name=Bi2021/> Highly effective but it is expensive. It can cause bronchospasm and it should be avoided in asthmatics. May cause diarrhea, fevers, or tachycardia.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lamba|first1=Akanksha|last2=Joshi|first2=Godawari|last3=Gupta|first3=Madhulika|date=2017-02-23|title=Role of carboprost in prevention of postpartum hemorrhage|url=https://www.ijrcog.org/index.php/ijrcog/article/view/1314|journal=International Journal of Reproduction, Contraception, Obstetrics and Gynecology|language=en|volume=5|issue=7|pages=2151–2154|doi=10.18203/2320-1770.ijrcog20162082|issn=2320-1789|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2020-10-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028061409/https://www.ijrcog.org/index.php/ijrcog/article/view/1314|url-status=live}}</ref>
*[[Misoprostol]] 600 to 1000 ug under the tongue, by mouth, or rectally.<ref name=Bi2021/> A synthetic [[Prostaglandin E1|prostaglandin E1 analog]] oral medication that can stimulate uterine contractions. Misoprostol does not need to be refrigerated because it is heat stable. It is easy to administer compared with oxytocin and ergot alkaloids in low-resource areas where refrigeration and sterile needles are not available.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Alfirevic|first1=Z.|last2=Blum|first2=J.|last3=Walraven|first3=G.|last4=Weeks|first4=A.|last5=Winikoff|first5=B.|date=2007|title=Prevention of postpartum hemorrhage with misoprostol|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1016/j.ijgo.2007.09.012|journal=International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics|language=en|volume=99|pages=S198–S201|doi=10.1016/j.ijgo.2007.09.012|pmid=17961574|s2cid=45977576|access-date=2020-10-22|archive-date=2021-08-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174413/https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1016/j.ijgo.2007.09.012|url-status=live}}</ref> May cause a low-grade fever.

Other options may include:
*[[Tranexamic acid]] 1 gram over 10 min<ref name=Bi2021/>
*[[Recombinant factor VIIa]] 50 to 100 ug/kg<ref name=Bi2021/>
* [[Carbetocin]] A synthetic analog of oxytocin, works similarly to oxytocin but the half-life is much longer.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rath|first=Werner|date=2009|title=Prevention of postpartum haemorrhage with the oxytocin analogue carbetocin|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0301211509004229|journal=European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology|language=en|volume=147|issue=1|pages=15–20|doi=10.1016/j.ejogrb.2009.06.018|pmid=19616358|access-date=2020-10-22|archive-date=2018-07-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180703130146/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0301211509004229|url-status=live}}</ref> It binds to smooth muscle receptors of the uterus, like oxytocin, and has been reported to produce a stable uterine contraction, followed by rhythmic contractions. It is not available in the US but is available in many countries for prevention of uterine atony and hemorrhage.
*[[Prostaglandin E2]] An alternative prostaglandin to misoprostol.<ref name=Coch2014/>

===Procedures===
[[File:UterusBallon1.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|An intrauterine balloon catheter is positioned on the center of two sheets of gauze impregnated with [[tranexamic acid]]]]
[[File:UterusBallon2.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|Device with balloon inflated with sterile water]]

After the medication is administered, the mother should be closely observed for to confirm the bleeding has stopped. If the bleeding has not stopped or physical exam does not show signs of restored uterine function within 30 minutes of medication administration, immediate invasive interventions are recommended.<ref name="pmid30197543">{{cite journal | vauthors = Songthamwat S, Songthamwat M | title = Uterine flexion suture: modified B-Lynch uterine compression suture for the treatment of uterine atony during cesarean section | journal = International Journal of Women's Health | volume = 10 | issue =  | pages = 487–492 | date = 2018| pmid = 30197543 | pmc = 6113941 | doi = 10.2147/IJWH.S170460 }}</ref><ref name=Stat2020/><ref name=":7">{{cite journal | vauthors = Songthamwat S, Songthamwat M | title = Uterine flexion suture: modified B-Lynch uterine compression suture for the treatment of uterine atony during cesarean section | language = English | journal = International Journal of Women's Health | volume = 10 | pages = 487–492 | date = 2018-08-24 | pmid = 30197543 | pmc = 6113941 | doi = 10.2147/ijwh.s170460 }}</ref>

[[Tamponade]] techniques include uterine packing (extending into the vagina) with gauze that also has a Foley catheter in place to allow for bladder drainage. It is inexpensive and readily available.<REF name=Stat2020/><ref name=":6" /> Balloon tamponade is the suggested method of tamponade in guidelines for management of PPH.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dahlke|first1=Joshua D.|last2=Mendez-Figueroa|first2=Hector|last3=Maggio|first3=Lindsay|last4=Hauspurg|first4=Alisse K.|last5=Sperling|first5=Jeffrey D.|last6=Chauhan|first6=Suneet P.|last7=Rouse|first7=Dwight J.|date=2015|title=Prevention and management of postpartum hemorrhage: a comparison of 4 national guidelines|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0002937815001593|journal=American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology|language=en|volume=213|issue=1|pages=76.e1–76.e10|doi=10.1016/j.ajog.2015.02.023|pmid=25731692|access-date=2020-10-22|archive-date=2020-05-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200505090117/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0002937815001593|url-status=live}}</ref> A [[bakri balloon]] to tamponade (also with vaginal packing) can be used with Foley catheter insertion to facilitate bladder drainage.<REF name=Stat2020/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Abraham C | title = Bakri balloon placement in the successful management of postpartum hemorrhage in a bicornuate uterus: A case report | journal = International Journal of Surgery Case Reports | volume = 31 | pages = 218–220 | date = 2017 | pmid = 28189983 | pmc = 5302184 | doi = 10.1016/j.ijscr.2017.01.055 | url = https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2210261217300585 | access-date = 2020-10-20 | archive-date = 2018-06-29 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180629214953/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2210261217300585 | url-status = live }}</ref> Vacuum-induced uterine tamponade is newer technique that uses low-level vacuum to evacuate blood from the uterine cavity and facilitate uterine contraction.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hofmeyr|first1=Gj|last2=Singata‐Madliki|first2=M|date=2020|title=Novel suction tube uterine tamponade for treating intractable postpartum haemorrhage: description of technique and report of three cases|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1471-0528.16169|journal=BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology|language=en|volume=127|issue=10|pages=1280–1283|doi=10.1111/1471-0528.16169|pmid=32043686|s2cid=211079411|issn=1470-0328}}</ref>

===Surgery===
Surgical management techniques include:
* Compression sutures such as the [[B-Lynch suture|B-Lynch]]<ref name=Stat2020 /><ref name=":7" />
*[[Curettage|Uterine curettage]] to remove retained placental products<ref name=Stat2020 /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Porreco|first1=Richard P.|last2=Stettler|first2=Robert W.|date=2010|title=Surgical Remedies for Postpartum Hemorrhage|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1097%2FGRF.0b013e3181cc4139|journal=Clinical Obstetrics and Gynecology|language=en|volume=53|issue=1|pages=182–195|doi=10.1097/GRF.0b013e3181cc4139|pmid=20142655|s2cid=1501779|issn=0009-9201|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2021-08-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210827174405/https://journals.lww.com/clinicalobgyn/Abstract/2010/03000/Surgical_Remedies_for_Postpartum_Hemorrhage.19.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>
* Uterine artery ligation, with or without ligation of the tubo-ovarian vessels. <ref name=Stat2020 /><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Shahin AY, Farghaly TA, Mohamed SA, Shokry M, Abd-El-Aal DE, Youssef MA | title = Bilateral uterine artery ligation plus B-Lynch procedure for atonic postpartum hemorrhage with placenta accreta | journal = International Journal of Gynaecology and Obstetrics | volume = 108 | issue = 3 | pages = 187–90 | date = March 2010 | pmid = 19944417 | doi = 10.1016/j.ijgo.2009.08.035 | s2cid = 9565057 | url = https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1016/j.ijgo.2009.08.035 | access-date = 2020-10-20 | archive-date = 2020-10-22 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201022194140/https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1016/j.ijgo.2009.08.035 | url-status = dead }}</ref> Ligation of the uterine and utero-ovarian arteries can decrease uterine bleeding by reducing the pressure of arterial blood flow in the uterus. It will not completely control the bleeding but may decrease blood loss while other interventions are being attempted.
* [[Internal iliac artery|Hypogastric artery]] ligation. Bilateral ligation of the internal iliac arteries reduces the pulse pressure of blood flowing to the uterus similar to uterine artery ligation. However, it is not a common procedure because of the degree of difficulty and risks.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clark|first1=Steven L.|last2=Phelan|first2=Jeffrey P.|last3=Yeh|first3=Sze-Ya|last4=Bruce|first4=Samuel R.|last5=Paul|first5=Richard H.|date=1985|title=Hypogastric Artery Ligation for Obstetric Hemorrhage|url=https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/Abstract/1985/09000/Hypogastric_Artery_Ligation_for_Obstetric.12.aspx|journal=Obstetrics & Gynecology|language=en-US|volume=66|issue=3|pages=353–356|pmid=3875064|issn=0029-7844|access-date=2020-10-22|archive-date=2020-10-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201026101246/https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/Abstract/1985/09000/Hypogastric_Artery_Ligation_for_Obstetric.12.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref>
* [[Hysterectomy]]

== Prognosis ==
Women with a history of PPH have a 2 to 3 times higher risk of PPH in their following pregnancies.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Oberg|first1=Anna Sara|last2=Hernandez-Diaz|first2=Sonia|last3=Palmsten|first3=Kristin|last4=Almqvist|first4=Catarina|last5=Bateman|first5=Brian T.|date=2014|title=Patterns of recurrence of postpartum hemorrhage in a large population-based cohort|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24351791|journal=American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology|volume=210|issue=3|pages=229.e1–8|doi=10.1016/j.ajog.2013.10.872|issn=1097-6868|pmc=3943527|pmid=24351791|access-date=2020-10-23|archive-date=2021-04-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210420104005/https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24351791/|url-status=live}}</ref><REF name=Stat2020/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Kominiarek MA, Kilpatrick SJ | title = Postpartum hemorrhage: a recurring pregnancy complication | journal = Seminars in Perinatology | volume = 31 | issue = 3 | pages = 159–66 | date = June 2007 | pmid = 17531897 | doi = 10.1053/j.semperi.2007.03.001 | url = https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0146000507000328 | access-date = 2020-10-20 | archive-date = 2018-06-11 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180611153725/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0146000507000328 | url-status = live }}</ref>

== Epidemiology ==
Uterine atony occurs during 1 in 40 births in the United States and is responsible for at least 80% of cases of postpartum hemorrhage.<REF name=Stat2020/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Abraham C | title = Bakri balloon placement in the successful management of postpartum hemorrhage in a bicornuate uterus: A case report | journal = International Journal of Surgery Case Reports | volume = 31 | pages = 218–220 | date = 2017-01-24 | pmid = 28189983 | pmc = 5302184 | doi = 10.1016/j.ijscr.2017.01.055 }}</ref><ref name=":9" />
